data.raw_text:
President Marcos’ performance rating is down? Well, well, well…this is sure sign that he’s doing the job he’s elected to do.

Despite being the only President in recent memory bold enough to drag two of the country’s biggest corruption rackets into the light—POGO and the multibillion-peso flood-control and infrastructure scandals—President Marcos Jr. still finds his performance ratings softening. And on the surface, that seems counter-intuitive. Exposing corruption should lift any leader’s numbers. But in the Philippines, political reality is rarely that simple.

For one, exposing a syndicate is only the first step. Once you shine a light on rot that has been festering for years, you inevitably expose not just criminals, but politicians, bureaucrats, and powerful backers who benefitted from the old, rotten system. These people won’t praise you for it—they will quietly (and sometimes openly) sabotage you. Every reform creates enemies, and every enemy fuels a counter-narrative designed to erode public confidence.

Second, the fallout from cleaning house is messy. Ordinary Filipinos may support anti-corruption efforts in principle, but they also feel the inconvenience and uncertainty that follow. Crackdowns create noise, hearings drag on, and the public—already fatigued by politics—sometimes mistake the chaos for incompetence. The President gets blamed for turbulence caused by the very corruption he is trying to dismantle.

Third, Marcos is governing in an age of disinformation. The same networks exposed in POGO, and now in the flood-control schemes, also operate online. They are skilled at hijacking public opinion—manufacturing outrage, twisting facts, and flooding social media with fake narratives. The moment Marcos turned away from Duterte-style governance, those machinery turned on him. And they haven’t stopped since. Just read all the fake news coming out of the Dutertes and their supporters. It’s quite extensive.

Finally, real reform takes time. When you clean up corruption, you delay projects, you halt illegal contracts, you audit agencies, and you freeze suspicious spending. (Thank God for presidential veto). All of these are good for the country—but they temporarily slow down visible results. Filipinos often want immediate relief. Mga walang pasensiya. The benefits of cleaning up POGO or flushing out infrastructure cartels won’t be felt overnight.

So yes, Marcos’ ratings may dip. But the dip doesn’t mean he’s doing nothing. In fact, it may mean the opposite. It may mean he’s shaking a system that has long protected the untouchable. Cleaning up a country as captured and compromised as the Philippines comes with a political cost.

And perhaps that’s the clearest sign that he’s actually doing the hard work. He is definitely working — and working smart. @bongbongmarcos @HouseofRepsPH 
@senatePH
